The work proposed a benchmark Bike-Bench that is unique and can be quite useful for rigorous study of generative models. It has a simulator that takes many hyperparameters as input to render bike images with various degree of subtlety, as well as 10K human ratings of these generated design, and 4K cyclist aerodynamics simulations. It also provides baselines of various classes (optimization, optimization-augmented generative models, etc) and specifies the pros and cons of these methods relatively clearly. The reviewers' feedbacks are also quite positive. Overall the work can be a good contribution to the community.

rebuttal.value:
We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and the recognition of the strengths and novelty of our benchmark. We generally agree with the discussed limitations, but have specific commentary below. 

> Regarding data, the original dataset shows imbalanced representation of certain parameters (like tube thickness). 

We acknowledge the dataset's bias in the tube thickness parameters, but feel that this bias actually serves to stress-test algorithms' ability to slightly deviate from the data distribution when necessary. In some senses, we consider this an accidental 'feature' of the benchmark. In reality, many datasets have similar systematic biases that must be overcome by successful generative models, so this is not unrealistic to benchmark.

>The design representation is limited to conventional bicycle structures

Regarding the parametric representation, we acknowledge the limited expressivity. However, we note that the representation is nonetheless expressive enough to reflect highly subjective elements of human perception and aesthetics, even if the highest-level topological structure of the bike is static. Regarding the decision to use parametric CAD, CAD is the industry standard in a majority of engineering design domains, where limited expressivity is desirable to avoid ambiguity. 

> For evaluation, geometric feasibility checks are not comprehensive.

We have designed an additional experiment to evaluate the ability of models to infer constraints that are not explicitly defined. We look forward to adding this experiment to the paper and hope this partially addresses the reviewer's concerns about non-comprehensive geometric feasibility checks. 

>Physical simulations (such as structural and aerodynamic assessments) are oversimplified with unrealistic assumptions that fail to fully reflect real-world complexity and diversity.

We agree that the physical simulations may exhibit some minor differences compared to real-world behavior due to simplifications. However these simplifications are well-informed and some of the simulations have even been verified through physical experimentation [1]. 

[1] Regenwetter, L., Weaver, C., & Ahmed, F. (2023). Framed: An AutoML approach for structural performance prediction of bicycle frames. Computer-Aided Design, 156, 103446.

> These biases may lead to benchmark results that don't fully align with actual engineering application scenarios.

We thank the reviewer for the comments. We agree that the mentioned biases and simplifications are key limitations that would cause minor inaccuracies, should a user build an AI-generated bike in practice. We have attempted to be fully transparent about these limitations in the paper, but maintain that these biases should have only minor effects on key takeaways in the context of generative model benchmarking.

We thank the reviewer for the positive feedback and insightful critiques. We are glad the reviewer sees value in the benchmark's tools and datasets and finds the benchmark design to be well-thought-out. We sincerely apologize for the maintenance issues with Harvard Dataverse, which have been out of our control during the reviewing period. It is our goal to make Bike-Bench as open and reproducible as possible. Had we anticipated these issues, we would have arranged an alternative dataset hosting. We offer itemized responses to the identified limitations and feedback below: 

>The paper has some serious reproducibility issues, as the main dataset URL doesn't work and the paper omits key implementation details.
>The URL provided is returning a 403 Forbidden error. Maybe you could upload it to Hugging Face instead?

We regretfully apologize for the issues and thank the reviewer for bringing this to our attention. Following the NeurIPS guidance on dataset hosting, we chose Harvard Dataverse as the only recommended platform that supports datasets over 300GB (Ours is 700). Dataverse also has many desirable features (DOI, version control, API access, etc.). Since Dataverse hosts many publicly-accessible datasets and was directly recommended by the conference, we did not expect issues with ease of access. However, Harvard Dataverse seems to be struggling after a recent update and, much to our frustration, Dataverse has had numerous downtimes (including during the reviewing window). Access issues also seem to vary depending on geographic location. Since other reviewers were able to access the data, this does not seem to be a universal problem. We agree with the suggestion to create a copy on Hugging Face for improved accessibility and are deciding the best approach to handle size constraints. However, per conference guidelines, we are unable to update the link during the reviewing period (or include any links in the rebuttal) to offer a more stable solution for the time being.

Regarding reproducibility: all evaluation, training, and scoring code is public and included in the submission-time state of the public repo (commit 87ddc89 in src/biked_commons/benchmark_models). Due to the volume of evaluation functions and number of methods tested, we avoided including excessive implementation details in the main paper. However, we are happy to add figures and extensive details on design evaluation, model training, and scoring to the appendix of the final paper to clarify any uncertainty about implementation. 

We have also significantly improved the documentation of the code, adding examples, installation guides, and example notebooks. While most of the recent improvements are internally implemented, we will bring the full updates to the public-facing repo after the reviewing period. 

>It isn't clear how well the findings will generalize, since the benchmark is limited to one type of bicycle frame and relies on simplified physics.
>I’d suggest the authors more clearly justify how insights from this bicycle task might transfer to other engineering domains.

Thanks for the feedback. Superficially, much of the benchmark is specific to the classic diamond-frame bicycle design. However, many of the design challenges incorporated into the benchmark are quite universal. The bike design problem is purely the mechanism to evaluate a model's ability to learn requirements grounded in ubiquitous design skills.  

To name a few examples: Geometric constraints exist in virtually any hardware design task. Mechanical loading on tube-based structures is seen in applications from car chassis design to assistive mobility walkers. Finally, intangible assessments of usability and subjective associations based on aesthetics are central to many product design tasks. 

We agree with the reviewer that these connections should be highlighted to help readers understand the ubiquity of the core design concepts at play. We will do so in the final paper. 

>The main conclusions feel a bit confirmatory, largely showing that optimizers are good at optimizing and LLMs struggle with structured numerical tasks.

Thanks for the observation. We agree that the initial results might largely align with readers' expectations. However, since Bike-Bench significantly extends beyond prior research, many of the findings are not obvious: 
* There is little research exploring parametric optimization using subjective human preference or textual/image guidelines. It is not obvious that heuristic or gradient-based parametric design optimization algorithms would be able to successfully adjust a design to match a text prompt, for example. 
* Based on existing literature evaluating 2-3 functional requirements on OAGMs, it is difficult to anticipate whether or not an OAGM can successfully satisfy 2 dozen simultaneously. 
* Few engineering design datasets are comprised of real design data rather than procedurally-generated randomized design configurations. This is the first time any design synthesis algorithm has been evaluated on a design problem with numerous multimodal constraints and real-world design data. 

In summary, though we agree that many of the findings may be intuitive, they have little scientific precedent and are far from an obvious confirmation of known results.

In addition, we have recently completed an additional experiment investigating how well models/algorithms are able to infer masked constraints from data (In real design problems, enumerating all possible constraints in closed form is typically impractical). These results illustrate clear cases in which generative models outperform optimization in optimality and validity (areas where optimization typically excels), a finding with little precedent in existing literature. We look forward to adding this result to the paper and hope this further alleviates the reviewer's concern. 

>It would be more constructive to explore advanced prompting techniques for LLMs, rather than simply confirming they perform poorly on this task.

Thanks for this suggestion. Our initial goal was to focus on comparisons of broad classes of methods, but we are planning some experiments to expand the LLM benchmarks, focusing on better prompting techniques (different context lengths, specialized handling of structured/tabular data, etc.). 

>The paper should also clarify the contribution of the 1.4M synthetic dataset, as its primary use seems limited to training a single surrogate model.

Thanks for the suggestion. Indeed, the dataset has extensive potential in supporting active research areas, such as text-to-CAD, image-to-CAD, etc; as well as many niche applications. While the current draft provides a cursory description, we agree that an expanded discussion of the broad variety of use cases would be helpful. We will gladly add this to the final paper.

More expressive modalities like images must eventually be converted to CAD to enable manufacturing, a task that is still impossible to reliably automate using state of the art methods. 

We also note that the representation is nonetheless expressive enough to reflect highly subjective elements of human perception and aesthetics. Additionally, through our rendering functionality, we allow an indirect pathway for models trained on free-form images to interact with Bike-Bench's tools. 

>The validity metric is defined as the proportion of all designs that simultaneously satisfy all constraints. While helpful, a metric giving the average constraint satisfaction in percent would help interpret the results better. 

Thanks for the suggestion. Our motivation to select this metric was largely based on convention. By convention, designs that violate **any** constraint are generally considered invalid, as they would be unsafe, impossible to manufacture, or have some other critical flaw regardless of how perfect the rest of the design is. However the average constraint satisfaction was one of several other interesting summary metrics (e.g. diversity, average novelty vs. dataset, etc.) that we were considering. An extra table of these metrics may be insightful, so we are happy to score and report these metrics in the final paper.

summary.value: This paper presents Bike-Bench, a new benchmark designed to evaluate generative models in the context of constrained engineering design, with a focus on bicycle design. The benchmark includes a synthetic dataset of 1.4 million parametric bicycle models, each accompanied by CAD files, images, and CLIP embeddings, along with 10,000 human-provided usability ratings. Bike-Bench assesses models across three key dimensions: validity (engineering feasibility), optimality (performance under multiple physics-based objectives), and similarity (aesthetic and structural resemblance). The evaluation spans 25 criteria, covering aspects such as aerodynamics, structural mechanics, ergonomics, and human perception. The authors benchmark a range of methods, including a large language model (OpenAI o4-mini), tabular generative models, optimization algorithms, and hybrid approaches. Results indicate that while tabular models perform best in similarity, optimization methods achieve higher scores in validity and optimality. Large language models, on the other hand, lag behind—likely due to their limited capacity for processing tabular data and complex constraints. Overall, Bike-Bench provides a rigorous and flexible framework for advancing generative AI in engineering design tasks that demand both functionality and manufacturability.

strengths_contributions.value:
The integration of constrained engineering design with generative modeling is an important and underexplored direction; this paper addresses that gap by introducing Bike-Bench, a benchmark tailored to real-world functional and manufacturable design tasks.


Beyond assessing distributional similarity, the benchmark evaluates designs across validity, optimality, and usability using 25 well-defined metrics grounded in multiphysics simulation, geometric constraints, and human-centered evaluation.


The authors provide a large, diverse, and richly annotated synthetic dataset of 1.4 million bicycle designs, along with human usability ratings and CLIP embeddings, offering broad support for a range of design generation tasks.

The paper benchmarks diverse model classes—including LLMs, tabular models, optimization-based methods, and hybrid systems—providing valuable insights into their respective strengths and limitations in design-oriented settings. Moreover, the conclusion section offers thoughtful analysis and reflections, highlighting areas for future improvement and directions for advancing generative design research.

The dataset and benchmark are well-documented and presented in a usable format, making it easy for future researchers to build upon this work.

limitations_weaknesses.value: One notable limitation of this work is the limited evaluation of large language models (LLMs)—only a single model, OpenAI’s o4-mini, is tested. As reported in Section 5, this model underperforms across most metrics; however, this may not fully reflect the potential of current LLMs. Evaluating a broader range of LLMs, including more powerful or specialized models with larger context windows or better support for structured/tabular data, could provide a more balanced and informative comparison. In particular, comparing reasoning-based （or not) models might reveal important differences in how LLMs handle constrained design reasoning tasks. This would offer deeper insight into the capabilities and limitations of LLMs in engineering design.

summary.value: This work introduces a benchmark for the task of designing bicycles. It consists of a large dataset and generator for bicycle designs. The designs are represented in parametric, CAD, and image-based formats.  Additionally, a set of design constraints and evaluators for the designs and further datasets that pair designs with performance evaluations, such as aerodynamics, usability ratings, and structural soundness are included. Lastly, methods are benchmarked in generating new bicycle designs in a conditional and unconditional setting.

strengths_contributions.value:
- This is a well rounded and comprehensive benchmark for designing bicycles with generative models. 
- The fact that the benchmark brings together a broad array of performance criteria enables novel research on combining different modalities as well multi-criteria optimization with deep learning.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
- The authors limit the design representation of generated designs to parametric descriptions of bicycles. They justify this choice as ensuring a direct CAD output can be generated from all designs. However, it also limits the potential expressivity of the design representation.
- The validity metric is defined as the proportion of all designs that simultaneously satisfy all constraints. While helpful, a metric giving the average constraint satisfaction in percent would help interpret the results better. 
- It would be good to include a table that gives a full overview over all elements included in the benchmark.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

dataset_code_comments.value: The code repository is not documented. There is no readme file or other form of documentation. Especially given the many different elements in the benchmark, this is definitely something the authors should change.

additional_feedback.value:
small comments
 - P. 2 'generative models must overcome their imprecise constraint satisfaction, ...' Instead 'engineers must overcome the limitations of generative models'. or 'generative models must be developed to overcome'
 - p. 2 'hybrid algorithms, that transcend boundaries' => just 'hybrid algorithms' would be clearer. There are a few more examples in the introduction, where the authors could remove superfluous descriptions to enhance clarity. 
 - p. 4 ' Each design is procedurally mapped to **to** a ....'
 - p. 8 discussion 'models must ... **tactfully** deviate from the distribution ...' Wrong choice of word

final_justification.value: I recommend a rating of 5 - accept. The benchmark is well rounded and comprehensively addresses a bicycle design task. Critical issues with documentation and accessibility of the benchmark were addressed by the authors during the rebuttal.

summary.value: This paper introduces Bike-Bench, a comprehensive new benchmark for evaluating generative models on the complex task of bicycle design. It assesses models on a mix of validity (constraint satisfaction), optimality (performance), and realism. The authors provide large new datasets and a full suite of evaluators, concluding that hybrid models combining generation and optimization perform best.

strengths_contributions.value:
1. The paper’s evaluation framework, which balances validity, optimality, and similarity, is a significant and well-thought-out contribution.
2. It's supported by impressive and versatile resources, including a massive synthetic dataset and a valuable human-rated usability dataset.
3. The benchmark is cleverly designed to be a non-trivial challenge, forcing models to satisfy physical constraints rather than just copying the training data.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
1. The paper has some serious reproducibility issues, as the main dataset URL doesn't work and the paper omits key implementation details.
2. It isn't clear how well the findings will generalize, since the benchmark is limited to one type of bicycle frame and relies on simplified physics.
3. The main conclusions feel a bit confirmatory, largely showing that optimizers are good at optimizing and LLMs struggle with structured numerical tasks.

ethical_considerations.value: No, there are no or only very minor ethics concerns

ethical_comments.value: The work adheres to ethical standards for human subject data collection.

dataset_code_comments.value: The URL provided is returning a 403 Forbidden error. Maybe you could upload it to Hugging Face instead?

additional_feedback.value:
1. I’d suggest the authors more clearly justify how insights from this bicycle task might transfer to other engineering domains.
2. It would be more constructive to explore advanced prompting techniques for LLMs, rather than simply confirming they perform poorly on this task.
3. The paper should also clarify the contribution of the 1.4M synthetic dataset, as its primary use seems limited to training a single surrogate model.

final_justification.value: I am recommending a rating of 4 (Borderline Accept). The paper's core contribution—a novel, large-scale benchmark for generative models in a constrained, multi-objective design space—is a clear and compelling reason to accept. However, this strength is significantly undermined by severe reproducibility flaws at the time of review. The inaccessibility of the primary dataset and the lack of code documentation are major weaknesses for a paper submitted to a Datasets and Benchmarks track. The authors' rebuttal promising future fixes is noted, but the review must assess the submission as is. Therefore, the paper's high potential is balanced against its current practical failings, making a borderline score the most appropriate.

summary.value:
This paper introduces Bike-Bench, a benchmark system for evaluating generative models on bicycle design under multiple objectives and constraints.

The researchers created multiple datasets, including 1.4 million synthetic bicycle designs and 10000 human-rated bicycle assessments, and designed 25 evaluation criteria covering geometric feasibility, structural soundness, aerodynamics, and more.

Through testing LLMs, tabular generative models, optimization-augmented generative models, and optimization algorithms, they found that LLMs and tabular generative models underperform compared to optimization and optimization-augmented generative models in validity and optimality, indicating significant room for improvement in generative AI for constrained multi-objective engineering design problems.

strengths_contributions.value:
This paper proposes the first engineering design benchmark focused on parametric designs, ensuring that generated designs map directly to CAD files, resulting in precise, manufacturable bicycle models.

Unlike existing CAD datasets, it includes 10 multidisciplinary design objectives and 15 design constraints, supported by rich evaluators leveraging physics simulation datasets, geometry engines, and real human assessment data.

It evaluates not only distributional similarity but also calculates validity and optimality scores, encouraging models to strategically deviate from the data distribution in targeted ways. Additionally, it supports benchmarking of tabular models, LLMs, design optimization algorithms, and hybrid algorithms, providing unprecedented opportunities for cross-category algorithm comparison.

limitations_weaknesses.value:
The main limitations of the Bike-Bench dataset include:

Regarding data, the original dataset shows imbalanced representation of certain parameters (like tube thickness) and the design representation is limited to conventional bicycle structures. 

For evaluation, geometric feasibility checks are not comprehensive, and physical simulations (such as structural and aerodynamic assessments) are oversimplified with unrealistic assumptions that fail to fully reflect real-world complexity and diversity.

These biases may lead to benchmark results that don't fully align with actual engineering application scenarios.

title.value: BikeBench: A Bicycle Design Benchmark for Generative Models with Objectives and Constraints

TLDR.value: We introduce a bicycle design benchmark that evaluates multiphysics performance, constraint satisfaction, and adherence to human preferences, and we benchmark LLMs, tabular generative models, and design optimization algorithms side by side.

abstract.value: We introduce BikeBench, an engineering design benchmark for evaluating generative models on problems with multiple real-world objectives and constraints. As generative AI's reach continues to grow, evaluating its capability to understand physical laws, human guidelines, and hard constraints grows increasingly important. Engineering product design lies at the intersection of these difficult tasks, providing new challenges for AI capabilities. BikeBench evaluates AI models' capabilities to generate bicycle designs that not only resemble the dataset, but meet specific performance objectives and constraints. To do so, BikeBench quantifies a variety of human-centered and multiphysics performance characteristics, such as aerodynamics, ergonomics, structural mechanics, human-rated usability, and similarity to subjective text or image prompts. Supporting the benchmark are several datasets of simulation results, a dataset of 10,000 human-rated bicycle assessments, and a synthetically generated dataset of 1.6M designs, each with a parametric, CAD/XML, SVG, and PNG representation. BikeBench is uniquely configured to evaluate tabular generative models, large language models (LLMs), design optimization, and hybrid algorithms side-by-side. Our experiments indicate that LLMs and tabular generative models fall short of hybrid GenAI+optimization algorithms in design quality, constraint satisfaction, and similarity scores, suggesting significant room for improvement. We hope that BikeBench, a first-of-its-kind benchmark, will help catalyze progress in generative AI for constrained multi-objective engineering design problems. We provide code, data, an interactive leaderboard, and other resources at https://github.com/Lyleregenwetter/BikeBench.
